text:
King's College London was founded in 1829, established as a rival institution to "London University" in response to theological controversy. Its foundation represented a Tory response aiming to reaffirm established educational values. The college opened in October 1831, initially having a senior and junior department, and later received affiliation with the emerging University of London in 1835. The King's College London Act 1882 changed the corporation from a proprietorial entity to a non-profit one and extended its objects to include the education of women, leading to the opening of the Ladies' Department in 1885.
Throughout the 20th century, King's College London experienced significant developments, including the opening of its own hospital in 1840, which later gained international recognition through the work of Joseph Lister. In 1910, the college merged into the University of London, losing its legal independence, though it regained legal independence in 1980. Key contributions include the discovery of the double helix structure of DNA in 1953. In 2006, King's College London was granted independent degree-awarding powers by the Privy Council, and it became a founding partner in the Francis Crick Institute in 2011. The university operates on five campuses in central London, including the Strand, Waterloo, Guy's, St. Thomas', and Denmark Hill Campuses.
